title: The clarinet's role in the ensemble
summary: Hall says his job is to fill in and keep out of the trombone's way, and he discusses trumpet and trombone styles that fit a Dixieland band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Then there's in relation to that too, when you play with the band and the ensemble, I wonder if you could describe a little bit what your idea of the clarinet part is. I remember asking about the part that the clarinet should play in the band, what's your job?

Well, my job is I try to fill in and I try to keep from running in to the trombone player. I tell you, that way you get the style. If you get guys that got ideas when you're jamming like that, you know what I mean? Like if the trombone is not running too much, a lot of times you see one guy will fit better in the Dixieland band than other guys.
Come on in if you like. We're just talking about clarinet style. You remember, how are you doing? How are you doing?
How are you doing? How are you doing?
Yeah, how are you doing? All right, fine.
We're talking about not running into the trombone part and so on.

Yeah, I try to keep from running the trombone part. That's the reason why you get a lot of guys like Tim. People would ask you, would you think he would fit in the Dixieland band? Or will this guy fit in the Dixieland band? A lot of times, this guy won't fit in the Dixieland band because what the trumpet player is doing, he's trying to play the same thing with clarinet is playing. You know, everybody is running. But when you get a good trumpet player, he still can go his way but play the melody. You know, play the melody. Every now and then he hits, you know what I mean, you know where you are. You see? But when you get a guy who forgets about the millions of other people, they're trying to explain, then you don't get anything.
As far as that was concerned, I had a question to ask you. When the trumpet is playing, more or less sticking straight to the melody, do you try to make your little runs more in the harmony part?

Yeah, you try to make your harmony part. And if you're used to playing like every night, usually if you just keep playing, you'll get that right note, you know. Maybe you may make some of them, you may make a bad note, you know. I mean, to the second, like he's playing melody, you're going to play the second. A lot of times, but you keep playing that tune, finally you get a note for note.
Would you say with any band, probably any band you play with, it takes a little while to get together?

Yeah, to get together. You just get about to tell what the next guy is going to do. Yeah, you get used to his style. Now you take Armstrong out, but of course, usually if he's playing a solo, if he's playing with a band, he practically plays the same way every night. Well, it's not hard to follow a guy like that. After you play with him for a while, you know what I mean, you find your notes and practically every time you play that same tune, it's the same way, you'll find your notes. You get the harmony part. Now you were saying that to keep out of the way of the trombone, does that mean to say that you don't want to play the same harmony part that the trombone?

The trombone is playing. And usually if you're playing note for note, you know what I mean, you're playing the same syncopation, you see. But a lot of times you get a trombone player, he's making a whole lot of stuff and it don't work in the Dixieland band.
Would you say more to the tailgates now?

Yeah, it fits in the Dixieland band. You take a guy like George Bronus, I tell you another guy is a good trombone player, fill in good, he's cutty cut short, he's got a good idea of music, you know. And a lot of times you start to play the tune, a lot of times the harmony is easy.
